v.rationale:
I ran all three test suites and they pass (26, 20 and 24 tests). I also ran a throwaway probe test in each implementation and then deleted it. It checked: a non-author sending an invalid payload, tag case, tags that differ only by whitespace, a null title on update, the CSRF behaviour outside the testing environment, a filter on an unknown tag, and a title that produces no slug.

impl-2 has a real production bug. Its API routes sit inside the 'web' middleware group, and with the environment switched out of testing, POST /api/posts returns 419 (CSRF). The suite hides this because Laravel skips CSRF checks during unit tests. It also has redundant trimming in prepareForValidation and an awkward UpdatePostRequest that extends StorePostRequest. That puts it clearly last.

impl-1 and impl-3 are close and share the same two minor flaws:
- A non-author sending an invalid payload gets 422 instead of 403, because the controller authorises after validation.
- Tag names are case-sensitive, so 'PHP' and 'php' become two tags.

impl-1 ranks first. It has separate Store and Update FormRequests, uses $request->enum() for the status filter, binds routes by slug, and uses ??= in the observer so factories can override the slug and published_at. Its 26 tests are the most thorough. Its weaknesses are a duplicated postAttributes() helper and an unnecessary Http::preventStrayRequests() in the tests.

impl-3 is a close second. Its nullable scopes keep the controller free of conditionals, its collection pipeline dedupes tags neatly, and its factory-based tests (hasAttached, sequence) are excellent. It loses a little for branching one request on isMethod('POST'), the tryFrom((string)) cast where $request->enum() exists, and a syncTagNames that both saves the tags and returns the reloaded model.

v.rationale: All three tests suites pass (impl-2: 20, impl-3: 24, impl-1: 26). They share the same core design: enum cast, #[Fillable]/#[ObservedBy]/#[Scope] attributes, an observer for the unique slug and published_at, a policy using user()->is(), and apiResource without show. My probes found the same behaviour in all three: blank tags return 422, title:null returns 422, an all-symbol title gets slug 'post' then 'post-2', client-supplied published_at/user_id are ignored, and an array passed to the filters returns 422. All three also validate before authorizing, so a non-author sending invalid data gets 422 instead of 403. Unauthenticated non-JSON requests return 500 (no login route) in all three; that comes from the base app. What separates them: impl-2 puts the 'web' middleware group on API routes, which brings in CSRF (PreventRequestForgery). The tests hide this because CSRF is skipped under unit tests, but real token-less JSON clients would get 419. impl-2 also has an awkward UpdatePostRequest that extends the store request and plucks parent::rules()['status'], and its trimming repeats TrimStrings, so it ranks last. impl-3 has the strongest tests and a very thin controller. Against that, its scopes take nullable arguments and no-op on null, syncTagNames mixes a side effect with a returned eager-load, and duplicate tags are silently dropped. impl-1 is the cleanest idiomatically: $request->enum(), ??= in the observer, slug route binding, 'sometimes','required' plus 'distinct' for explicit 422s, and a policy whose delete delegates to update. Its only real flaws are minor ceremony (a postAttributes() helper copied into both requests, Http::preventStrayRequests, a trivial cast test), so it ranks first, narrowly ahead of impl-3.

v.rationale:
All three versions do the job and behave almost the same. Every test suite passes (18, 17 and 17 tests). The probes found no real bugs in any of them. They covered malformed --days values (1.5, empty, -1, 007), a non-interactive production run without --force, dry-run while locked, the lock being released after an exception, and a real permission-denied file deletion. In every case each version kept the row, carried on with the rest and exited 1. Each one has a Cache::lock inside the command plus onOneServer, deletes through lazyById, and indexes created_at. The ranking comes down to idiom and the quality of the tests.

impl-1 has the most idiomatic code. It uses ConfirmableTrait and select(['id','path'])->lazyById, and its code is the leanest. Its weak points are a hardcoded Europe/Copenhagen timezone nobody asked for, a 1-hour lock, and no test for an operator confirming. 

impl-3 has the cleanest tests for the confirmation path and a more realistic 6-hour lock. But it writes its own confirmation logic instead of using ConfirmableTrait and adds a redundant withoutOverlapping. 

impl-2 is nearly identical to impl-1 in code. Its tests rely on a heavy subclass-and-copied-signature workaround to test the prompt, and leave a dead mock expectation behind, so it ranks last.

v.rationale: All three versions have nearly the same design: a #[Scope] scope with a created_at index, lazyById, a Cache::lock shared with manual runs, onOneServer, dry-run before confirmation, and keeping the row when the file can't be deleted. All test suites pass (17, 17 and 18 tests). I ran four throwaway probes against each version, then deleted them. Three passed for all three versions: a real permission-denied directory on a local disk (row kept, the rest processed, exit 1), more than 1000 failing rows followed by one good row (no infinite loop with lazyById), and --days=0 and --days=1.5. The fourth probe, production with -n, could not run in PHPUnit because the mocked console output doesn't respect -n. I ran it on the real CLI instead, against a temporary SQLite database: all three refuse with exit code 1. The seeded export row wasn't created in that run (the setup step failed quietly), so the CLI checked only the exit codes, not whether rows were kept; the in-suite tests cover that. impl-2 ranks first: it uses ConfirmableTrait as intended, returns INVALID for bad --days, has broad tests (both confirmation answers, -n refusal, a mock of the Filesystem contract) and no bugs; its main flaw is the anonymous command subclass used to test confirmation. impl-3 has equally sound behaviour and cleaner tests, but it hand-rolls production confirmation instead of using ConfirmableTrait. impl-1 adds a Europe/Copenhagen timezone nobody asked for, so the job runs at 02:00 UTC instead of 03:00. It also uses a by-reference closure with a partially selected model, swaps the Storage facade for duck-typed anonymous classes in its tests, and has no test for the interactive 'yes' path.

All three implementations are nearly identical in their core logic. Each adds the same #[Scope] inactiveFor with a grouped whereNull/orWhere on '<' now()->subDays, a datetime cast, a nullable timestamp migration, an attribute-based command validated with filter_var, and Schedule::command()->dailyAt('06:00')->appendOutputTo(). None of them adds onOneServer, which is correct for a single server. All test suites pass. I probed each one with these --days values: 0, '', ' 7', '+7', '007', very large numbers, and a future login. Behaviour matched across all three, except that impl-2 rejects 0 while impl-1 and impl-3 accept it. Neither choice is wrong. I found no functional bugs in the counting logic.

The ranking comes down to test quality and small choices. impl-2 has the most thorough tests: exact output, a deterministic boundary via travelTo(startOfSecond), and checks on the schedule's timezone and output path. Against that, it hardcodes an unrequested Europe/Copenhagen timezone on a UTC app, leaves a duplicate commented line in Pest.php, and prints '1 users'. impl-1 has the leanest and most modern code ($this->fail(), no extra factory state), but its loose ': 1' substring assertions weaken its tests. impl-3 is clean, but its schedule test does not check the log output, it includes a low-value schema test, and it freezes time inconsistently. Overall: impl-2 > impl-1 > impl-3, with small margins between them.

v.rationale: All three pass their suites and share a sound design (Redis-backed onOneServer, ShouldBeUnique hourly job, Copenhagen timezone, batched cart deletes). The differences come from crash recovery. When I killed a sync job mid-run (lock left behind), impl-1 and impl-2 (UniqueFor 3600) dropped the next hourly dispatch. impl-3 (UniqueFor 3300) let it through. impl-1 and impl-3 also give their commands overlap locks with short expiries; I confirmed both locks can be taken again once expiry passes. impl-2 has no overlap lock, so nothing can get stuck. That is defensible, but its tests forbid overlap locks outright. impl-3 also has the strongest scheduler tests, including two schedule:run ticks in the same minute, and the most current conventions. It is ranked first. impl-1 is second: it has bounded overlap locks and a schedule:run test, but it has the dropped-hour bug, leaves the cache and queue on database instead of Redis in .env.example, and has a test that asserts nothing. impl-2 is third: it has the same dropped-hour bug and no end-to-end scheduler test, though its daylight-saving datasets and single-query batched delete are good. All three raise the shared Redis retry_after to suit one job.

v.rationale:
I ranked them impl-3, then impl-2, then impl-1. All three pass their own test suites (impl-2: 28 tests, impl-3: 22, impl-1: 17). The edge-case probes were removed afterwards.

**What all three get right**
- **Exactly once across servers:** every task uses onOneServer.
- **Copenhagen time:** a minute-by-minute probe over both DST days found exactly one prune run per day in each implementation.
- **Crash recovery for the commands:** none of them can be blocked for a day. impl-2 skips withoutOverlapping altogether. impl-1 and impl-3 give it short expiries, and a probe confirmed that a lock left by a killed run expires in time.

**What separates them: the hourly SyncSupplierStock lock**
- If a worker is killed mid-run, the job's unique lock is never released and only times out.
- impl-1 and impl-2 time it out after a full hour (UniqueFor 3600). If the next hourly dispatch fires a few seconds earlier than the previous one did, the stale lock is still held. A probe that dispatched at 10:00:05 saw the 11:00 run skipped in both.
- impl-3 uses Timeout 3000 < UniqueFor 3300 < retry_after 3600, so the lock always expires before the next tick. It also adds FailOnTimeout and sets SCHEDULE_CACHE_STORE=redis explicitly. Its only real defect is cosmetic: the email says '1 orders'.

**impl-2 vs impl-3**
- impl-2 has the simplest, most idiomatic code (a LIMITed delete loop) and the best schedule tests (isDue checked at explicit UTC instants for winter and summer).
- Its one real bug is the lost hourly run after a crash, which puts it second.

**Why impl-1 is last**
- It has the same lost-hour lock problem as impl-2.
- Its retry_after (3700) is longer than UniqueFor, so a redelivered dead job can fail and release the lock held by the next job.
- Its .env.example doesn't point the cache and queue at Redis, so its retry_after setting has no effect with that template.
- Weaker details: a filler expect(true)->toBeTrue() test, a concrete Carbon type hint, and the verbose weekly()->mondays()->at().
